title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Welcome!

A science course, taught in English
Real biology, and the English that scientists use to talk about it
Today: the course, your teacher, and you


Plan about 20-25 minutes for this session, then move on to How to Study. Speak slowly and clearly, and use gestures and the board: for many students this is the first lesson fully in English. Reassure them that they are not expected to understand every word.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Who Am I?




Marco Chiapello
I studied biology at the University of Turin, and have a PhD in Fungal Biology and Biotechnology.
I worked in research and teaching in Italy, the UK, and the Switzerland.
Currently I work at Agilent Technologies, a life sciences, diagnostics, and analytical laboratory technology company. It helps scientists and laboratories measure, analyze, diagnose, and understand chemical and biological samples.















Keep it short and personal: a photo of your lab, your field work, or an object from your work makes it concrete. Students are curious about what a scientist actually does all day.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Guess the Fact
Two of these are true, one is false. Which one is the lie?

My English grade in high school was 4/10.
I am currently working only in English.
I am working in a biology laboratory.


Students vote with their hands (1, 2 or 3) before you reveal the answer. Ask a few students to explain their choice in English: “I think number 2 is false, because…”. This models the game they will play next.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Now It’s Your Turn

Move from the teacher to the students. The goal is that everyone says at least one sentence in English today.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Introduce Yourself
Say these three things:

My name is …
One thing I like is …
One word that describes me is …
What I want to be when I grow up is …


Go around the room quickly, about 20 seconds per student. Write the sentence frames on the board. If the class is large, do it in groups of four and then ask one student per group to introduce someone else (“This is Marco, he likes…”).

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Find Someone Who …



has been to an English-speaking country



wants to study medicine or biology



has watched a science documentary this month



can name a famous scientist (not Einstein!)



knows what DNA stands for





Give 5 minutes. Rule: they can only ask in English (“Have you ever…?”, “Do you want to…?”). At the end, ask who completed the most rows and check a few answers with the class. The DNA question is a nice bridge to the course content: deoxyribonucleic acid.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:

Ask: which topic looks most interesting to you? Which one is a mystery? Point out the lab session (4) and the forensic session (8), which students usually look forward to.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
How Each Lesson Works

Live quiz on the previous lesson (scan the QR code)
New topic: slides, videos, activities
Material page on the website: vocabulary and reading to review at home


Show the course website on the projector and where to find the sessions. Explain that the quiz is practice, not a grade: it tells them and you what to review. The first quiz will be at the start of the next lesson, on How to Study.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Assessment

The final exam is multiple choice plus a short answer section
It will be in 2027
Live quizzes are practice: they show what to review


Fill in according to the school’s arrangement. Be clear and concrete: students want to know what counts.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Class Agreements

English first: try in English, then ask for help
Questions are welcome: there are no stupid questions in science
Phones for quizzes and activities only
Respect: listen and help each other


Ask the class if they want to add an agreement. Mistakes in English are normal and welcome, just like failed experiments in science.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Getting to Know You




Scan and answer 5 short questions:

Your English confidence (1–5)
Your favourite science topic
What you want to learn



Give 3 minutes. The answers help you adapt the level of English and the examples to this class. This is also a test run of the QR code system used for the quizzes, so any phone or connection problem shows up now instead of during the first quiz.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Let’s Start!
Next: How to Study

Transition to Session 1. A natural bridge: “In this course you will learn a lot of new things. So, first of all: how do we learn?”

title: How to Study
text:
How to Study

Study strategies backed by cognitive science
Some habits feel productive but do not produce lasting learning
Today: prepare your body and mind, avoid what does not work, learn six strategies that do


Open by asking how they currently study: highlighting, re-reading notes, cramming the night before? Ask who has used flashcards. Do not judge the answers. The goal is to find out what actually works, not what feels productive.

title: How to Study
text:
Goals of the Project

Improve learning for students
Understand how we learn
Improve education and science
Propose strategies based on scientific evidence


These materials come from the Learning Scientists, a group of cognitive psychologists (Yana Weinstein and Megan Smith, with illustrator Oliver Caviglioli), funded by the APS Fund for Teaching and Public Understanding of Psychological Science. Point out the source so students see this is research, not opinion. Full references are on the session material page.

title: How to Study
section: Your Brain Is Part of Your Body
text:
Your Brain Is Part of Your Body






This sets up the next two slides: learning is a physical process. Sleep, exercise and food affect memory and attention, so preparing your body is part of studying. Ask: when did you last study well after a bad night of sleep?

title: How to Study
text:
Preparing Your Body and Mind (1/2)



Keep a sleep schedule: the more regular it is, the easier it is to fall asleep and wake up
Build a wind-down routine so your body learns that it is time to rest
Put your phone away before bed: interacting with it keeps your mind active when it should be winding down





Ask students to estimate how many hours they sleep and when they put the phone away. Keep it non-judgmental. Connect to memory: memories are consolidated during sleep, so an all-nighter before an exam weakens recall the next day.

title: How to Study
text:
Preparing Your Body and Mind (2/2)



Exercise regularly: good for physical and mental health
Stay hydrated: dehydration hurts your ability to think and remember
Eat healthy snacks: fruit and vegetables while you study, because thinking is hard work





Quick poll: how many of you drank water during the last lesson? Make the point that studying is physically demanding, so it is worth looking after yourself. Do not go beyond the claims on the slide.

title: How to Study
text:
The Myth of Multitasking

This is the most important correction in the session. Name the myth and ask what students think it means before showing the next slide.

title: How to Study
text:
What Is Multitasking?



The term is misleading
We do not do several tasks at once: we switch between them
A few minutes of study, then TV, then texting, then back to study
Our attention can only be on one task at any given time





Ask: when you say you are studying while listening to music, what happens when a notification arrives? Each switch costs time and attention, so the study time is split and less is learned. Ask students to name their own switching habits.

title: How to Study
text:
Focusing Your Learning (1/2)



Stick to a routine: it puts you in a studying state of mind. Choose something you find pleasant and relaxing
Try the Pomodoro technique: focused work in short blocks of about 25 minutes, with a short break in between





Pomodoro means “tomato” in Italian: the original timer was a tomato-shaped kitchen timer. Ask students to try one 25-minute block this week and report back at the next session.

title: How to Study
text:
Focusing Your Learning (2/2)

Use apps to reduce distractions on your phone and computer (for example Cold Turkey or Forest)
Create accountability groups with peers: studying in pairs or groups makes it easier to stay on task


Cold Turkey blocks distracting websites; Forest grows a virtual tree while you stay off your phone. For accountability: everyone works on their own assignment, but in the same room, so you are less tempted to drift.

title: How to Study
text:
Avoid Strategies That Don’t Work

Students often rely on methods that feel productive but produce weak long-term learning. The next slides show which ones, and how to make them more effective.

title: How to Study
section: Popular Strategies: How to Make Them Work (1/2)
text:
Popular Strategies: How to Make Them Work (1/2)



Re-reading builds confidence but not much learning. Combine it with spaced and retrieval practice
Flashcards are powerful when you use them to recall from memory, not just to read. Keep testing yourself even after a correct answer





Re-reading feels fluent, so students mistake fluency for learning. Demonstrate the difference: read a paragraph, close the book and write what you remember, then compare. The gap is where the learning happens.

title: How to Study
section: Popular Strategies: How to Make Them Work (2/2)
text:
Popular Strategies: How to Make Them Work (2/2)

Note-taking: complete notes that capture the main concepts, summarised in your own words (the Cornell method)
Outlining: read the material twice. The first time, do nothing else. The second time, record the main points


The Cornell method: a notes column, a cue column with questions, and a summary at the bottom. The outlining trick separates understanding from extracting. The next few slides show how to set up Cornell notes. Connect back to the six strategies: these are variants of retrieval practice and elaboration.

title: How to Study
text:
Cornell Note-Taking
A simple page layout that turns your notes into a study tool

Introduce the Cornell method as the concrete version of the note-taking tip from the previous slide. It was developed at Cornell University in the 1950s. The goal of this short section is that students can set up a Cornell page in their notebook this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Cornell Notes: The Page Layout




Cue columnkeywords and questions


Notes columnmain ideas, facts, examples, drawings


Summary: the whole page in 2-3 sentences, in your own words






A Cornell page, filled in




Draw this on the board or show a real notebook page. Left column about one third of the width, notes on the right, summary in a strip at the bottom. Leave the cue column and summary empty during the lesson: they are filled in afterwards.

title: How to Study
text:
Cornell Notes: Five Steps

Record: take notes in the right column during the lesson, in your own words
Question: after class, write questions and keywords in the cue column
Recite: cover the notes column and answer each cue from memory
Summarize: write the main idea of the page in the bottom box
Review: come back to the page after a few days and again after a few weeks


Steps 1 and 4 are note-taking and elaboration. Step 3 is retrieval practice and step 5 is spaced practice, so the Cornell method already combines several of the six strategies we are about to see. Ask students which step they think is the most useful, and which they are most likely to skip (usually step 3).

title: How to Study
text:
Cornell Notes: Example







Cue column
Notes column




What is a hypothesis?
A testable, falsifiable explanation for an observation


Why a control group?
Baseline for comparison, shows the effect of the treatment


Precision vs. accuracy?
Precision: repeated results agree. Accuracy: close to the true value



Summary: A good experiment changes one variable and compares it with a control.

Use content from the next lesson so students see it is practical. Stress that the cues are real questions that you could answer out loud, not single words.

title: How to Study
text:
Cornell Notes: Hold On!

Do not copy the teacher or the book word for word: rewrite in your own words
Write cues that are questions, not just titles
Do not skip step 3: reading the notes again is not retrieval, covering them and answering is
Fill in the cue column and summary the same day, while you still remember the lesson


Link to the “Hold on” warnings of retrieval practice and elaboration that come later. Homework suggestion: use the Cornell layout for the notes of the next lesson.

title: How to Study
text:
Cornell Notes: A Full Example



Cornell notes on this lesson: How to Study



This page shows what a student’s Cornell notes on today’s lesson could look like. Point out the three zones: the questions on the left are written after class, the notes on the right during class, and the summary at the bottom last. Challenge: cover the right column and answer each question from memory.

title: How to Study
text:
Six Strategies for Effective Learning



Learning Scientists: Six Strategies for Effective Learning



This is the overview of the six strategies we will study: retrieval practice, spaced practice, dual coding, interleaving, concrete examples and elaboration. Each strategy has a “How to do it” part and “Hold on” warnings. The highlighted hexagon in each section shows which strategy you are looking at.

title: How to Study
text:
Retrieval Practice






Retrieval practice means bringing information to mind, not just looking at it. It is the strategy with the strongest support in the research, so give it time in the session.

title: How to Study
text:
Retrieval Practice: Video


The Learning Scientists, “Retrieval Practice: A video for Students”. Play it in class, then ask students to name one way they could use the strategy this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Retrieval Practice: Write or Sketch






Put away your class materials, write or sketch everything you know, then check the materials for what you missed.

title: How to Study
text:
Retrieval Practice: Trade Tests






Take as many practice tests as you can. If there are none, make your own and trade with a friend.

title: How to Study
text:
Retrieval Practice: Flashcards






Flashcards work when you practise recalling the answer, and go beyond definitions to links between ideas. Ask students to try a three-minute blank-page recall of today’s lesson now, then compare with the slides.

title: How to Study
section: Retrieval Practice: Hold On! (check your materials)
text:
Retrieval Practice: Hold On! (check your materials)






Retrieval works best when you check your materials afterwards.

title: How to Study
section: Retrieval Practice: Hold On! (retrieval is hard)
text:
Retrieval Practice: Hold On! (retrieval is hard)






Retrieval is supposed to feel hard. Stress that struggling is evidence the strategy is working.

title: How to Study
section: Retrieval Practice: Hold On! (more than definitions)
text:
Retrieval Practice: Hold On! (more than definitions)






Warn against recalling only definitions: students should also recall main ideas, relationships and new examples.

title: How to Study
text:
Spaced Practice






Spaced practice means spreading study over time instead of cramming. Start with the slide’s example: five hours spread over two weeks works better than five hours in one go.

title: How to Study
text:
Spaced Practice: Video


The Learning Scientists, “Study Strategies: Spaced Practice”. Play it in class, then ask students to name one way they could use the strategy this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Spaced Practice: Plan Early






Start planning early for exams and set aside a little time every day. Ask students how they could spread their revision this week.

title: How to Study
section: Spaced Practice: Review After a Delay
text:
Spaced Practice: Review After a Delay






Review each lesson after a delay, not right after class.

title: How to Study
text:
Spaced Practice: Revisit Older Material






After reviewing the most recent class, go back to important older material from a week or a month ago. Ask students when they last reviewed the lesson from the previous session.

title: How to Study
section: Spaced Practice: Hold On! (sit down with strategies)
text:
Spaced Practice: Hold On! (sit down with strategies)






When you sit down to study, use effective strategies rather than just re-reading your notes.

title: How to Study
section: Spaced Practice: Hold On! (forgetting is useful)
text:
Spaced Practice: Hold On! (forgetting is useful)






Feeling that you forget things from day to day is normal and useful: having to retrieve the memory is what strengthens it.

title: How to Study
section: Spaced Practice: Hold On! (small spaces add up)
text:
Spaced Practice: Hold On! (small spaces add up)






Small spaced sessions of a few days each add up to much more than one long session.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding






Dual coding means combining words and visuals. Using both gives you two ways to retrieve the same idea.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Video


The Learning Scientists, “Dual Coding: A Video For Students”. Play it in class, then ask students to name one way they could use the strategy this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Find the Visuals






Look at your class materials and find the visuals. Compare them with the words.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Explain the Visual






Look at a visual and explain in your own words what it means.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Draw Your Own






Take information you are trying to learn and draw visuals to go along with it.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Hold On! (many formats)






Try different ways to represent the information visually: an infographic, a timeline, a cartoon strip, a diagram or a graphic organizer. You can skip the next examples if you are short on time.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Infographic






An infographic combines a few numbers, short labels and simple shapes.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Timeline






A timeline is useful for history: events in order, with dates.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Cartoon Strip






A cartoon strip works well for a sequence of steps, such as a process.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Diagram






A diagram shows parts that work together, for example the organs of the body in biology.

title: How to Study
text:
Dual Coding: Graphic Organizer






A graphic organizer shows how ideas are linked. Ask which format suits each subject best.

title: How to Study
section: Dual Coding: Hold On! (draw from memory)
text:
Dual Coding: Hold On! (draw from memory)






Work up to drawing from memory. Start with the class material open, then close it and draw what you remember.

title: How to Study
text:
Interleaving






Interleaving means switching between different topics during a study session, instead of studying one topic until it is finished.

title: How to Study
text:
Interleaving: Video


The Learning Scientists, “Interleaving: A Video for Students”. Play it in class, then ask students to name one way they could use the strategy this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Interleaving: Switch Between Topics






Study topic A, then B, then C. Do not study one idea for too long.

title: How to Study
text:
Interleaving: Mix the Order






Go back over the ideas in different orders in later study sessions to strengthen understanding.

title: How to Study
text:
Interleaving: Link the Ideas






Make links between different ideas as you switch between them.

title: How to Study
section: Interleaving: Hold On! (do not switch too often)
text:
Interleaving: Hold On! (do not switch too often)






Switching is good, but not so often that you spend too little time on any one idea. You need to understand each one.

title: How to Study
text:
Interleaving: Hold On! (it feels harder)






Interleaving will feel harder than blocking, and that is the point. Ask students to suggest how they could interleave their revision for two subjects this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Concrete Examples






Concrete examples means using specific cases to understand abstract ideas. Ask students for a concrete example of a concept from this course.

title: How to Study
text:
Concrete Examples: Video


The Learning Scientists, “Concrete Examples: A Video for Students”. Play it in class, then ask students to name one way they could use the strategy this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Concrete Examples: Collect Them






Collect the examples your teacher uses, and look in your class materials for more.

title: How to Study
text:
Concrete Examples: Link Each One






Make the link between the idea and each example, so you understand how the example applies.

title: How to Study
text:
Concrete Examples: Share Them






Share examples with friends and explain them to each other.

title: How to Study
text:
Concrete Examples: Hold On! (check examples)






Not every example you find online is used correctly. Check examples with the teacher.

title: How to Study
section: Concrete Examples: Hold On! (make your own)
text:
Concrete Examples: Hold On! (make your own)






The strongest examples are the ones you create yourself.

title: How to Study
text:
Elaboration






Elaboration means explaining and describing ideas with many details. Ask a question about why something works, then find the answer and explain it to a classmate.

title: How to Study
text:
Elaboration: Video


The Learning Scientists, “Elaboration: A Video for Students”. Play it in class, then ask students to name one way they could use the strategy this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Elaboration: Ask Why and How






Ask yourself “how” and “why” questions while studying, then find the answers in the class materials and discuss them with classmates.

title: How to Study
text:
Elaboration: Connect Ideas






Take two ideas and ask how they are similar and different. This forces you to explain how they work together.

title: How to Study
text:
Elaboration: Use Your Own Experience






Link new ideas to your own experiences. Ask for a personal example from the class.

title: How to Study
text:
Elaboration: Hold On! (accuracy)






Elaborations must be accurate, so check them against the class materials or ask the teacher.

title: How to Study
text:
Elaboration: Hold On! (explain without notes)






You should be able to explain without looking at your notes. That is what turns elaboration into retrieval practice.

title: How to Study
text:
Bonus: NotebookLM
A Google AI tool that is a great study partner

Introduce the last tool of the session. The question to ask students: is this AI helping me learn, or doing the learning for me? Everything in this section is about the first.

title: How to Study
text:
What Is NotebookLM?



Made by Google, free with a Google account
You upload your own sources: class slides, PDFs, notes, web pages
Answers come from your documents, with citations you can check





Check the current features and any school restrictions before the lesson at notebooklm.google.com, since Google updates the tool often. For students under 18, confirm the school’s policy on Google accounts and AI tools. Show the interface live if possible.

title: How to Study
section: Two Ways to Use an AI
text:
Two Ways to Use an AI



AI writes for you
AI helps you learn




“Write my essay on DNA”
“Quiz me on DNA, one question at a time”


You copy, and learn nothing
You answer, and the AI checks


The thinking happens in the AI
The thinking happens in your head


Weak retention
Retrieval practice, elaboration, spacing




Ask: which of these two columns is the homework? The left column produces a text you do not understand. The right column produces understanding you can use in the exam. The AI should be the study partner, not the author.

title: How to Study
text:
NotebookLM for Learning: Four Prompts

“Quiz me on this chapter, one question at a time. Wait for my answer before you continue.”
“I will explain photosynthesis in my own words. Point out what I missed, using only my sources.”
“Make flashcards from my notes. I will recall first, then check.”
“Give me a concept map with blanks, and ask me to fill in the links.”


Each prompt turns the tool into retrieval practice or elaboration. Model one prompt live with a passage from the class materials, then ask a student to try another. Stress: “using only my sources” keeps the answers accurate.

title: How to Study
text:
NotebookLM: Rules of Use

Your brain does the work: answer before you look at the AI’s answer
Check against the sources: citations let you verify every claim
Never hand in AI text as your own writing: use it to understand, then write yourself


Connect back to the myth of multitasking and to retrieval practice: the best prompt is one that makes you recall, not one that gives you the answer. Ask students for an example of a prompt they would use this week.

title: How to Study
text:
Recap

Prepare your body and mind: sleep, exercise, water, healthy snacks
Multitasking is switching; attention can only be on one thing at a time
Re-reading and cramming feel productive but work poorly
Six strategies: retrieval practice, spaced practice, dual coding, interleaving, concrete examples, elaboration
NotebookLM can be a study partner, as long as you do the thinking

title: How to Study
text:
Most study habits feel productive, but only some of them lead to lasting learning. This session covers how to prepare your body and mind, which common strategies to avoid, and six evidence-based strategies that work. Read through the material below, then watch the presentation.
→ View the slides

title: How to Study
text:
Most study habits feel productive, but only some of them lead to lasting learning. This session covers how to prepare your body and mind, which common strategies to avoid, and six evidence-based strategies that work. Read through the material below, then watch the presentation.
→ View the slides

title: How to Study
text:
Key Vocabulary

Retrieval practice — bringing information to mind from memory (closing the book and writing or sketching what you know), rather than re-reading it.


Spaced practice — spreading study over time, with gaps between sessions, instead of cramming.


Dual coding — combining words and visuals (diagrams, timelines, drawings) to represent the same information.


Interleaving — switching between different topics or types of problems during a study session, instead of studying one topic until it is finished.


Concrete examples — specific cases that illustrate an abstract idea.


Elaboration — explaining an idea in detail, asking how and why it works, and connecting it to what you already know.


Multitasking — the myth of doing several tasks at once. In practice we switch rapidly between tasks, and attention can only be on one task at a time.


Pomodoro technique — studying in focused blocks (about 25 minutes) separated by short breaks.

title: How to Study
text:
Further Reading
These are the sources cited in the original presentations, from the Learning Scientists (learningscientists.org):

Retrieval practice: Roediger, H. L., Putnam, A. L., & Smith, M. A. (2011). Ten benefits of testing and their applications to educational practice.
Spaced practice: Benjamin, A. S., & Tullis, J. (2010). What makes distributed practice effective? Cognitive Psychology, 61, 228–247.
Dual coding: Mayer, R. E., & Anderson, R. B. (1992). The instructive animation: Helping students build connections between words and pictures in multimedia learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 4 (as printed in the original slide; please verify the volume), 444–452.
Interleaving: Rohrer, D. (2012). Interleaving helps students distinguish among similar concepts. Educational Psychology Review, 24, 355–367.
Concrete examples: Rawson, K. A., Thomas, R. C., & Jacoby, L. L. (2014). The power of examples: Illustrative examples enhance conceptual learning of declarative concepts. Educational Psychology Review, 27, 483–504.
Elaboration: McDaniel, M. A., & Donnelly, C. M. (1996). Learning with analogy and elaborative interrogation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 88, 508–519.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
What is this course?
Scientific English is a science course taught entirely in English. We look at real biology (the scientific method, DNA, biotechnology, bioinformatics, evolution and plants) and, at the same time, we learn the English that scientists use to describe it.
You do not need perfect English to take part. Mistakes are part of learning a language, just as failed experiments are part of science. What matters is that you try to speak, read and write in English every lesson.

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Your teacher
Marco Chiapello — I studied biology at the University of Turin, and have a PhD in Fungal Biology and Biotechnology. I worked in research and teaching in Italy, the UK, and Switzerland. I currently work at Agilent Technologies, a life sciences, diagnostics, and analytical laboratory technology company that helps scientists and laboratories measure, analyze, diagnose, and understand chemical and biological samples.

Contact: chiapello.m@gmail.com

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Class agreements

English first: try in English, then ask for help if you are stuck
Questions are welcome, at any time: there are no stupid questions in science
Phones are for the quizzes and activities, not for social media
Respect: listen when someone is speaking and help each other

title: Welcome to Scientific English
text:
Useful classroom English

Could you repeat that, please? — when you did not hear or understand.


How do you say … in English? — when you know the word in Italian but not in English.


What does … mean? — when you do not know a word.


Can you speak more slowly, please? — when the speaker is too fast.


I agree / I disagree, because … — to give your opinion in a discussion.


I’m not sure, but I think … — to answer even when you are not certain.
